answers.text: Tell the assistant: read the supplier's email and always give me back exactly three lines, in this order - the delivery date, then the item and quantity, then any change from the original order, nothing else added. This works because I told it to always give three lines in that order.
Tell it to take the week's expense lines and put each one into a table with the date, amount, category and who submitted it, then sort it so it's easy to read through before it goes to the memo.
Something about the dates in that email doesn't sit right with me. I'd want someone to look it over before it goes out to the client.

I checked the delivery numbers - 62 against 54 last week does look about right for the increase. I'm not confident on the rest of it, I'd want someone in ops to go over the figures before this gets sent up.
I'd go with the second one, it shows the actual sales and returns numbers so you can see where the 4.1% comes from. The first one is just a number with nothing behind it.
I'd send the second reply, it has the order reference and the credit reference so you can actually look it up. The first one just says sorry and gives a credit without saying which order or how much.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. No, better safe than sorry. 5. No.
The pricing and discount numbers I'd leave out of it, that feels like something we shouldn't be pasting into a tool we haven't cleared. The rest of it I'm not so sure about.
Before I send the weekly report to my manager, I go back and check the delivery and stock totals against the source spreadsheet - just a quick cross-check of the main numbers.

I'd put a check at the end, step 4, before the confirmation goes out automatically, since that's the point you can't take back. The extraction step at the start could also cause problems if it reads the order wrong in the first place.
